locator.heading: Campion, Wild

source_text:
_Descript._] THE wild White Campion has many long and somewhat broad
dark green leaves lying upon the ground, and divers ribs therein,
somewhat like plantain, but somewhat hairy, broader, but not so long.
The hairy stalks rise up in the middle of them three or four feet high,
and sometimes more, with divers great white joints at several places
thereon, and two such like leaves thereat up to the top, sending forth
branches at several joints also; all which bear on several foot-stalks
white flowers at the tops of them, consisting of five broad pointed
leaves, every one cut in on the end unto the middle, making them seem
to be two a-piece, smelling somewhat sweet, and each of them standing
in a large green striped hairy husk, large and round below next to the
stalk. The seed is small and greyish in the hard heads that come up
afterwards. The root is white and long, spreading divers fangs in the
ground.

The Red wild Campion grows in the same manner as the White; but its
leaves are not so plainly ribbed, somewhat shorter, rounder, and more
woolly in handling. The flowers are of the same form and bigness; but
in some of a pale, in others of a bright red colour, cut in at the ends
more finely, which makes the leaves look more in number than the other.
The seeds and the roots are alike, the roots of both sorts abiding many
years.

There are forty-five kinds of Campion more, those of them which are of
a physical use, having the like virtues with those above described,
which I take to be the two chief kinds.

_Place._] They grow commonly through this land by fields and
hedge-sides, and ditches.

_Time._] They flower in Summer, some earlier than others, and some
abiding longer than others.

_Government and virtues._] They belong to Saturn, and it is found by
experience, that the decoction of the herb, either in white or red wine
being drank, doth stay inward bleedings, and applied outwardly it does
the like; and being drank, helps to expel urine, being stopped, and
gravel and stone in the reins and kidneys. Two drams of the seed drank
in wine, purges the body of choleric humours, and helps those that are
stung by scorpions, or other venomous beasts, and may be as effectual
for the plague. It is of very good use in old sores, ulcers, cankers,
fistulas, and the like, to cleanse and heat them, by consuming the
moist humours falling into them and correcting the putrefaction of
humours offending them.

pubmed.title: Veratrole biosynthesis in white campion.
pubmed.relevance_note: Describes chemical biosynthesis of veratrole, lacking clinical data on digestive or immune support.

pubmed.title: Tetracycline but not sulfamethazine inhibits early root growth of wild grassland species, while seed germination is hardly affected by either antibiotic.
pubmed.relevance_note: Examines antibiotic effects on root growth, irrelevant to human therapeutic applications.

evidence.summary: Modern literature focuses on heavy metal accumulation and plant biochemistry rather than the traditional claims for digestive aid or scurvy prevention. No direct evidence supports efficacy for stomach weakness or appetite loss in current databases.

pubmed.title: The Sister Chromatid Division of the Heteromorphic Sex Chromosomes in Silene Species and Their Transmissibility towards the Mitosis.
pubmed.relevance_note: Focuses on cytogenetics, not pharmacological effects for traditional uses.

pubmed.title: Identification and properties of UDP-glucose: cyanidin-3-O-glucosyltransferase isolated from petals of the red campion (Silene dioica).
pubmed.relevance_note: Describes enzyme properties in petals, lacking data on renal or anti-venom efficacy.

pubmed.title: Identification, properties, and genetic control of UDP-glucose: cyanidin-3-rhamnosyl-(1 leads to 6)-glucoside-5-O-glucosyltransferase isolated from petals of the red campion (Silene dioica).
pubmed.relevance_note: Details pigment biosynthesis, with no mention of treating kidney stones or venom.

evidence.summary: Modern literature retrieved for Silene dioica focuses on cytogenetics and petal enzyme characterization. No contemporary clinical trials or pharmacological studies were found supporting traditional claims regarding kidney stones, plague, choleric humours, venomous bites, urinary retention, or internal bleeding.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence (PMIDs: 40862352, 23547102) focuses on thallium accumulation and flavonoid biosynthesis. No clinical data supports historical claims for bleeding, stones, or plague prevention; cytotoxicity of heavy metals in *S. latifolia* poses safety risks.
concordance.uncertainty: Low uncertainty regarding lack of therapeutic efficacy based on current literature search.
caveats: Historical context differs from modern pharmacology.
No EMA approval for these indications.

issues: Grade 'D' is unearned: The entry lacks any EMA approval or clinical evidence for the historical indications (bleeding, stones, plague), yet the rationale cites cytotoxicity risks without explicitly flagging the lack of therapeutic efficacy as a primary reason for rejection in the graph schema. The grade implies a specific level of negative validation that requires explicit citation of failed trials or regulatory rejections, which are absent; only 'no data' is present. Additionally, the 'contradicts' direction is weakly supported by mere absence of modern clinical data rather than direct contradiction by evidence.
